threads.thread_goal: Align on incident scenarios, scope, and playbook structure.

messages.text: Team, let's kick off the Crisis Communication Playbook project. The goal is to create a clear, actionable guide for on-site security incidents. First up, we need to define the scope. I suggest we start by mapping the most critical incident scenarios as per T1. I've put together a preliminary list to get us started: 1. Physical altercation, 2. Medical emergency, 3. Unauthorized access/trespassing, 4. On-site protest, 5. Fire/evacuation. Thoughts?

Great start, @286680. That list covers the most common situations. From a community relations perspective, the 'On-site protest' scenario is particularly important to get right. We should ensure the messaging is focused on de-escalation and safety for everyone involved.

The list looks solid. I'd also suggest we add a scenario for 'Data breach or critical system failure' that has an on-site component. It might seem technical, but it often requires immediate on-site communication to manage access and employee concerns.
I agree with @143124. Having a system failure scenario would be very helpful. We've had close calls with that in the past.

Good point. A tech incident with physical impact is a critical gap. Let's add 'Critical system failure' to the list. That gives us six to start with. Any objections to locking this in as our priority list for v1?
what about theft? that happens a lot.

That's a valid point, @47290. For v1, we're focusing on incidents that require broad, multi-channel communication. We can classify internal theft under 'Unauthorized access' for now and build out more specific procedures later. The key is to cover events that pose a significant safety or reputational risk first.
ok
The list of six scenarios works for me. It's comprehensive but manageable.

Excellent. DECISION: We will prioritize these six scenarios for the v1 playbook: 1. Physical altercation, 2. Medical emergency, 3. Unauthorized access/trespassing, 4. On-site protest, 5. Fire/evacuation, 6. Critical system failure.

Next, let's talk structure for the playbook itself, which is part of T2. I propose a simple, modular structure: Section 1: General Principles & Roles. Section 2: Incident-Specific Checklists (one for each scenario). Section 3: Communication Templates (Internal, Media, Stakeholder). Section 4: Post-Incident Review. How does that sound?
That structure makes sense. It's logical and easy to navigate. For Section 1, we should include the Stakeholder and Contact Matrix from A8 to make it actionable.
I like it. It's very clear. I can take the lead on drafting the content for the training materials that would support this, which would fit into a sub-section or an appendix.

Good call on including A8. Let's formalize ownership. I can take Section 1 (Principles/Roles). @143124 and @409854, can you two co-own Section 3 (Templates)? @47537, you're perfect for the training materials. I'll handle the incident checklists in Section 2 for now, with input from @47290 on operational realities.
Works for me. @143124 and I can divide and conquer the templates.
Sounds good. I'll sync with @409854.
sure i can help
Perfect. DECISION: The playbook will follow the four-section structure discussed, and we have confirmed the owners for each part.
Great kickoff, everyone. We have our scenarios and a clear structure. Let's get moving on the initial drafts.

threads.thread_goal: Define on-site escalation scripts and quick-reference checklists.

messages.text: Hi team, I've drafted a first version of the On-Site Incident Escalation Checklist (A2) based on our agreed scenarios. The goal is to make this extremely simple and clear for staff under pressure. See the attached doc. I've focused on the first 3 steps: Assess, Secure, Report. @47290, could you give this a look from a security guard's perspective? Is this realistic?
i looked at it. the report section says to call the operations manager. we usually just radio the security supervisor first. is that changing?

Excellent catch, @47290. That's exactly the kind of detail we need. The process shouldn't change existing, effective protocols. I'll update it to say 'Report to Security Supervisor via radio', who then escalates to the Ops Manager. Thank you.

This is a great, clean draft. My only suggestion would be to add simple icons next to each step (e.g., an eye for 'Assess', a lock for 'Secure', a phone for 'Report'). Visual cues can significantly improve comprehension during stressful situations. It's a technique we use in teaching materials all the time.
Looks good. At what point in this checklist does the communications team get notified? Should that be an explicit step?

Good question. The Ops Manager is responsible for activating the crisis comms team. I'll add a note under the escalation step to make that clear: 'Ops Manager to activate Crisis Comms Playbook'. And @47537, love the icon idea. I'll incorporate that.

Okay, I've updated the draft of A2 with all the feedback: corrected reporting chain, added icons, and clarified the comms team activation point. Here is v2. If there are no further objections, I'd like to approve this version for the playbook.
v2 looks great. Clear, concise, and practical. I approve.
The new version is excellent. Approved.
looks much better now. thanks.
Fantastic. DECISION: The final version of the on-site incident escalation checklist (A2) is approved.
Now for the practical side, as part of T8. How do we make this available to on-site staff? Should we have laminated printouts, a digital version on company phones/tablets, or both?
has to be printed. a laminated card that fits in your pocket. phones can die or break. we need something that always works.

I agree with @47290 on the physical copy. A reliable, non-digital backup is essential. However, a digital version is also valuable for quick updates and for staff who are more desk-based. I'd propose we do both.
Both makes sense. We can push updates to the digital version instantly and then refresh the printed cards quarterly.
Agreed. Both it is. DECISION: The checklist will be available as both a laminated printed card for on-site staff and a digital version accessible on company devices.
Great work here, team. I'll take the action to get the final design for A2 formatted for both print and digital.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on media holding statements, Q&A, and channel strategy.

messages.text: Hi all, as part of T4 and T7, @409854 and I have drafted the initial Media Holding Statements (A3) and the Multi-Channel Crisis Communication Strategy (A5). Please find the documents linked here for your review. We've tried to create a baseline statement for each of the six scenarios we agreed on.
Feedback is welcome, especially on the tone and the proposed approval flows in A5. We want it to be fast but also safe.

Thanks for getting these drafts out. I've done a quick review. The statements in A3 are a solid foundation. For the 'On-site protest' scenario, I'd suggest we rephrase 'We are monitoring the situation' to 'Our priority is the safety of everyone involved, and we are working to ensure a peaceful resolution'. It's more active and empathetic. Also, in A5, the approval flow for social media updates seems a bit slow. For minor updates, can we empower the on-call PR lead to post without waiting for legal?

I strongly agree with @286680's suggestion on the protest language. It shifts the focus to safety, which is exactly right. For the channel strategy in A5, we should also explicitly define when we use internal channels versus public ones to avoid employees hearing news from the media first.

Excellent points, @286680. We'll revise the protest statement. Regarding the approval flow, we were being cautious, but I agree we can create a tiered system. We can define 'minor updates' as those that stick to pre-approved facts and let the PR lead handle them, with legal sign-off required only for new messaging. How does that sound?
A tiered system is the perfect solution. That gives us both speed and control.
i dont know much about media stuff but the statements seem ok to me
Good point on internal vs external, @47537. We'll add a section to A5 that specifies an 'internal-first' principle for any news directly impacting employees.

Okay, @143124 and I have updated both documents with the feedback. The revised A3 and A5 are now in the folder. The holding statements are refined, and the channel strategy includes the tiered approval flow and the internal-first principle.
The new versions look great. Let's make a decision on these. Can we agree on these revised statements as the default for each scenario?
Yes, I approve of the holding statements.
Approved from my side.
Great. DECISION: The default holding statement for each priority incident scenario in A3 is approved.
And what about the multi-channel strategy and approval flow in A5? Any final thoughts before we lock that in?
I think it's ready. The tiered approach gives us the flexibility we need.
It looks good to me. The internal-first principle is a key addition.
Excellent. DECISION: The multi-channel crisis communication strategy and approval flow (A5) are approved.
Great. The next step for T4 is to get the final legal review on these statements. I'll take that action item.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize internal briefing templates and training approach.

messages.text: Hello everyone. I've drafted the Internal Staff Briefing Templates (A4) and an outline for the training session content, covering T5 and T6. My approach was to keep the language extremely simple, clear, and reassuring. The template in A4 uses a 'What Happened, What We're Doing, What You Need to Do' structure. The training outline focuses on interactive role-playing. Your feedback would be appreciated.

This is outstanding, @47537. The structure is perfect—it directly answers the three questions everyone has in a crisis. The tone is spot-on. No notes on the template itself, it's ready to go. The role-playing idea for training is also much more effective than a simple presentation.
This is really well done. The template is easy to follow. For the training, how much time should we allocate for these sessions?
Thanks! I've designed the core content to fit within 45 minutes, leaving 15 minutes for Q&A, so a 60-minute slot per session as specified in T6.
role playing sounds better than just listening to someone talk.
I agree with everyone, this is excellent work. The template is clear and empathetic.
Thank you all for the positive feedback. Shall we formally approve the internal briefing template format and tone?
Absolutely. DECISION: The internal staff briefing template format and tone as documented in A4 are approved.

Wonderful. Now for the training delivery. I see a few options: we could run live sessions for all staff, provide a recording, or do a mix—live sessions for high-impact groups like security and front-line staff, and a recording for everyone else. The mixed approach is often most effective. What are your thoughts?

The mixed approach is the most pragmatic and resource-efficient. The interactive element is crucial for the staff who will actually use the playbook, so live sessions for them are a must. A recording works well for general awareness for the rest of the company.
I agree, the mixed approach is best. It lets us prioritize the hands-on training for the people who need it most.
Great, it seems we have consensus. We also need to think about the simulation drills mentioned in T9 and A6. The live training sessions would be a perfect precursor to those.
Let's lock it in. DECISION: The training will use a mixed format: mandatory live sessions for security and front-line staff, with a recording available for all other employees.
Perfect. I will take the next step of drafting a schedule for the live sessions and coordinating with the relevant department heads.

threads.thread_goal: Close out project with review process and distribution plan.

messages.text: Team, we're approaching our deadline. All the core components are now complete. I've consolidated everything into the final Crisis Communication Playbook v1.0 (A1). Before we roll this out, let's do a final check on our readiness and close out the remaining tasks.

Looks great all together! For T10, the Post-Incident Review Procedure (A7) is complete and has been shared with the security and communication team leads. It outlines the steps for a debrief within 48 hours of any incident.
The first live training session for the security team is scheduled for next Tuesday. The materials are all set and we've done a dry run.
The legal team has given their final sign-off on all media-facing templates. We're clear from a compliance standpoint.
we got the new laminated checklists yesterday. they look good.
Excellent progress on all fronts. The final piece is the distribution plan for the full playbook (T12). What's our strategy for getting A1 into the right hands?

I propose a two-pronged approach. First, an email to all stakeholders on the contact matrix with a link to the final document in a read-only shared folder. Second, @286680 and I can do a 15-minute briefing for senior management to walk them through the high-level process.
That sounds like a solid plan. It ensures everyone is aware and that leadership understands the value. Let's proceed with that.
The plan sounds great. This has been a fantastic team effort.

I agree. Thank you all for your hard work and collaboration. We've created a robust and practical tool that will make a real difference. Let's remember that this is a living document; the post-incident review process (A7) will be key to keeping it effective.
Great work everyone!
thanks everyone
Alright, I'm marking this project as complete. The next phase is implementation and continuous improvement. Well done.
